Gone matte and chalky with no shine left on it anywhere, a postbox-red bucket sits upturned at the base of a fresh turret — the turret still darker and drum-hard where the bucket left it, a single razor shell pressed into its base.

Faded to pale salmon on its sun side only and still cadmium yellow on the other, a plastic shovel stands dead vertical in the notched top of the near wall, its blade driven in up to the handle, handle cropped by the frame's upper edge.

With sand ground permanently into every moulded seam, a cobalt-blue bucket perches on top of an unlifted tower, its rolled rim sitting flush against the packed wet sand beneath it, one small mussel shell dropped inside visible through its open base.

The gloss scoured right off one flank by years of grit, a hot-orange bucket is tipped on its side in the spoil heap, pale dry sand spilled out of it in a low heap and running loose across the darker packed surface below.

Gone milky and fogged where the sun has got at it, a turquoise plastic shovel lies flat across the canal as a bridge, its blade resting on the far cut face, drifted sand already building in thin pale lines along its upper edge.

Worn back to pale bare plastic at the rim and still deep plum everywhere below, a bucket is hooked over a turret by its handle, one side pressed hard against the wet-cut tower face, the other hanging free above the moat's dark floor.

Sun-faded on one side only, the facing flank gone nearly white while the reverse holds its acid green, a plastic shovel is driven blade-first into the dam at a steep angle, the blade gone entirely into the packed sand, only the handle remaining above.

Crazed with a fine net of hairline cracks across its whole lower half, a postbox-red plastic rake lies dragged across the outer slope, its tines leaving a field of parallel grooves in the pale dry sand running off toward the frame's right edge.

Gone soft-edged and rounded where it has been dragged across wet sand for a season, a cadmium-yellow bucket is buried to its rim in the ramp, the rolled rim and one arc of handle the only parts above the surface, sand packed hard against them.

The paint of a printed pattern gone leaving only a faint ghost of former colour on its flank, a cobalt-blue small watering can stands in the moat, water risen halfway up it, its spout angled out over the dark still surface between the walls.

Sand ground permanently into every moulded seam, a hot-orange plastic sieve sits half-buried at the base of the near wall, its mesh clogged solid with wet compacted sand, every hole dark and sealed, the rim just proud of the surrounding surface.

Gone matte and chalky with no shine left on it anywhere, an acid-green wooden spoon stands upright in the open top of a small turret, its handle straight and vertical, a thread of dry weed caught tight under the bowl where it meets the rim.

The gloss scoured right off one flank by years of grit, a turquoise driftwood plank lies over the moat, its ends bedded into the packed wet sand on both sides, the dark wet line of the moat cutting cleanly beneath it between the two walls.

Gone milky and fogged where the sun has got at it, a deep-plum plastic shovel lies down on the wet sand beside the finished wall, its own pressed shape left in the surface where it has been lying, the impression dark and sharp-edged.

Worn back to pale bare plastic at the rim and deep orange below, a plastic rake is wedged upright against the outer face of the near tower, its tines resting against the cut sand, handle leaning out and cropped hard by the frame's left edge.

Faded to pale coral on its sun side and still postbox-red on the sheltered face, a bucket and a cadmium-yellow shovel rest together at the tower's base — the bucket turned away so only its scoured back faces the camera, the shovel half-buried blade-first beside it.

Sun-faded on one side only, one face gone to washed-out turquoise while the reverse still holds its acid green, a small watering can stands upturned at the mouth of the finished canal, its base upward, dry sand sifting off its domed underside in thin pale streams.

Crazed with a fine net of hairline cracks sealed at one point with a tight wrap of orange twine, a cobalt-blue bucket sits upturned at the base of a run of eight bucket-cast turrets ranged abreast along the wall from edge to edge, its rolled rim sitting level on the packed dark sand.

Gone soft-edged and rounded where it has been dragged repeatedly through grit, a hot-orange plastic shovel is laid blade-down in the spoil heap, its handle angled up and then cropped by the top of the frame, wet sand packed in along the ribbed underside of the blade.

Furred all over with dried sand and gone stiff with salt, a length of cadmium-yellow twine runs along the top of the near wall between two shovels planted at either end, the twine going taut then sagging slightly at its middle, its fibres furred with clinging dry grains.

The paint of a printed pattern gone leaving only a ghost of what had been vivid on its face, a postbox-red plastic sieve leans against the inner wall of the moat, its clogged mesh turned across the frame from side to side, the dark wet sand packed flush against every stopped hole.

Gone matte and chalky with no shine anywhere on it, a deep-plum bucket sits upturned at the base of a newly released turret, the turret still near-black and drum-hard above it, a score of identical turrets ranged abreast along the wall from edge to edge behind, each one paling as it dries.

The gloss scoured right off one flank by years of grit, a turquoise plastic shovel stands in the notched top of the dam, its blade sunk into the gap, handle rising straight and cropped by the upper frame edge, wet sand pressed tight into the ribbed faces of the blade.

Worn back to pale bare plastic at every edge, still acid-green in the deep moulded centre, a pennant of bright hot-orange plastic twists edge-on on a drinking straw planted in the highest turret, curling and rippling rather than lying flat, its shadow falling thin across the cut wet face below.

Gone milky and fogged where the sun has reached it, a cadmium-yellow bucket and a postbox-red plastic rake rest at the dam's outer base — the bucket tipped on its side with dry sand spilling from it, the rake turned away and half-buried, its tines pressed into the packed surface.
